introduction_markdown:
**Cameroon General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. Geography 2 (0750), Paper 2, ADVANCED LEVEL, JUNE 2024. Duration: THREE HOURS.**

Instructions to candidates: Answer FOUR questions, choosing at least ONE from each Section.

All questions carry twenty-five marks each. You are encouraged to refer to specific examples drawn from any part of the world. Credit will be given for such specific examples.

Only the required number of questions will be marked.

Marks will be awarded for well annotated maps and diagrams where these are relevant.

You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers.
incertitudes: Question 1 c) : les régimes cités (Nyong, Ntem, Lobe, Sanaga, Wouri, Mungo, Meme, Benue, Logone, mayos du Nord) et leurs périodes de hautes eaux sont donnés de mémoire à titre d'ordre de grandeur (« about ») ; ils sont reconnus mais à faire relire. Les ouvrages Song Loulou, Edea (Sanaga) et Lagdo (Benue) sont des barrages existants.
Question 1 b) : la mention du lac Tchad et de la mer d'Aral comme exemples d'assèchement lié aux prélèvements est classique mais simplifiée (le lac Tchad est aussi influencé par le climat).

Aucun corrigé officiel : les corrigés sont des réponses modèles rédigées de mémoire, sans accès à une source. Les exemples cités (lieux, programmes, institutions) sont des exemples reconnus ; les chiffres sont des ordres de grandeur donnés avec « about » ou « more than ». Les faits cités sont à faire relire par un géographe avant toute mise en avant.

Règle de choix : le sujet impose « Answer FOUR questions, choosing at least ONE from each Section » (Section A : questions 1 à 3, Section B : questions 4 à 6, Section C : question 7 seule). `regles_choix` porte le minimum imposé par section (`parmi 1 sur 3` pour A et B, `parmi 1 sur 1` pour C) ; la règle « 4 questions en tout » n'est pas exprimable en entier et est recopiée dans `introduction_markdown`. La question 7 offre deux versions (EITHER / OR) de trois sous-questions : codées « a », « b », « c » (EITHER) et « OR-a », « OR-b », « OR-c » (OR), reliées par une règle `ou`.

Sujet scanné de cinq pages (page de garde, deux pages de questions, une page de planche de carte topographique 1:50 000 « Dufftown » avec ses signes conventionnels, puis le fond de carte du Cameroun pour la question 3c i). Page de garde vérifiée : ADVANCED LEVEL, Geography, Paper 2, code 0750, JUNE 2024, Three Hours. Filigranes gcerevision.com ignorés. La planche topographique (page 4) appartient aux épreuves de cartographie (Paper 3) et ne sert à aucune question de ce Paper 2 : non transcrite. Seul le fond de carte du Cameroun (page 5) est utilisé (question 3).

Points : chaque question est imprimée à 25 marks et les sous-parties somment bien à 25 (Q1 8+8+9, Q2 6+10+9, Q3 8+8+(3+6=9), Q4 6+10+9, Q5 5+9+11, Q6 8+9+8, Q7 EITHER 9+8+8, OR 6+10+9). Aucun écart avec le sujet. Le sujet imprime des marks pour un ensemble de sous-points (ex. Q1 a (i)+(ii) = 8 marks) : le corrigé les regroupe sous une seule sous-question.

questions.enonce_markdown:
a) Distinguish between:

(i) The processes of convection and conduction of energy transfer from the Earth's surface to the atmosphere.

(ii) Tropical Continental and Tropical Monsoon climates.

(8 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Conduction and convection (4 marks)**

The Earth's surface is heated by short-wave solar radiation. The warm surface passes energy to the atmosphere in two main ways (as well as by long-wave radiation and by the latent heat of evaporation).

| | **Conduction** | **Convection** |
|---|---|---|
| **What happens** | Direct transfer of heat by molecular contact: the warm ground heats the thin layer of air touching it. | Transfer of heat by the vertical movement of masses of air (and moisture): the heated air expands, becomes less dense and rises, and cooler, denser air sinks to replace it. |
| **Distance** | Only the lowest centimetres or metres of the air, because air is a very poor conductor. | The whole depth of the troposphere (several kilometres). |
| **Importance** | Minor for the atmosphere as a whole, but it is the first step: it warms the air layer next to the ground, and at night the cold ground cools that layer (radiation fog, frost). | The main way in which heat (including latent heat released when vapour condenses) is carried upwards; it forms cumulus and cumulonimbus clouds, low-pressure cells and convectional rainfall, and is strongest over hot land in the afternoon in the tropics. |

In short, conduction is transfer by contact over a very short distance, while convection is transfer by the large-scale rising and sinking of air.

**(ii) Tropical Continental and Tropical Monsoon climates (4 marks)**

| | **Tropical Continental (Sudan or Sahel type)** | **Tropical Monsoon** |
|---|---|---|
| **Location** | Interiors of continents about 10 to 20 degrees from the equator, away from the sea (e.g. the Sahel and Sudan zone of West Africa; in Cameroon, the Far North and North, such as Maroua and Garoua). | Tropical coasts and windward lands exposed to a seasonal reversal of winds (e.g. the Indian sub-continent, Bangladesh, South-East Asia; the Guinea coast of West Africa and the coast of Cameroon around Douala and Limbe show a monsoon-type regime). |
| **Air masses and winds** | Wet tropical maritime air from the south-west for a short time in summer; for the rest of the year dry, dusty tropical continental air (the Harmattan) from the Sahara. | The summer monsoon brings warm, very humid maritime air onshore; in the dry season the winds are offshore and dry. |
| **Rainfall** | Low and unreliable (about 500 to 1,000 mm), in one short wet season of about 3 to 5 months; a long dry season of 6 to 8 months. | High (often 1,500 to 3,000 mm or more, and over 4,000 mm on windward mountain slopes), in a long wet season of 6 to 9 months; a short dry season of 1 to 3 months. |
| **Temperature** | Very hot, with a large annual range and a large daily range in the dry season (hottest in the months before the rains). | Hot, but with a smaller range: the cloud and rain of the monsoon keep the wet season cooler. |
| **Natural vegetation** | Savanna grassland and thorn scrub with scattered drought-resistant trees. | Monsoon forest (semi-deciduous) and, in the wettest places, evergreen forest; mangroves on the coast. |

questions.enonce_markdown:
b) Explain how any **three** different human activities on the Earth's surface would affect the drainage basin hydrological cycle.

(8 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
The drainage basin hydrological cycle is a system of stores (vegetation, soil, groundwater, rivers) and flows (interception, infiltration, throughflow, overland flow, evapotranspiration, baseflow). Human activities change the stores and flows. Three activities are explained (about 2.5 marks each, with a short conclusion).

**1. Deforestation.** Removing the trees reduces **interception** and **evapotranspiration**, and the roots no longer bind the soil or create channels for water. More rain reaches the ground directly, the soil is compacted and capped by the rain, so **infiltration falls and overland flow increases**. Water reaches the channel faster, so the storm hydrograph has a steeper rising limb, a **higher peak and a shorter lag time**, and floods are more frequent. Less water enters the groundwater store, so **baseflow is lower** in the dry season, and the faster flow carries more sediment, which silts up rivers and reservoirs. (Afforestation has the opposite effect.)

**2. Urbanisation.** Roofs, roads and pavements are **impermeable**: infiltration, soil storage and evapotranspiration are cut. Gutters, drains and sewers carry the water straight to the river, so **surface runoff increases and lag time falls**: the hydrograph is flashy, with a high peak and flash floods (a serious problem in towns such as Douala and Yaounde in the rainy season). Groundwater recharge is reduced, and the river carries pollutants from the roads and waste.

**3. Dam construction and irrigation (water abstraction).** A dam stores water in a reservoir, which **regulates the river regime**: flood peaks are reduced and dry-season flow is increased, but evaporation from the large water surface increases and the flow, and sediment, downstream are reduced. Irrigation, and the pumping of groundwater by wells and boreholes, remove water from rivers and from the water table (the **water table falls**), and part of the water is returned to the atmosphere by evapotranspiration; where abstraction is heavy, rivers shrink or dry up (as in the case of Lake Chad and the Aral Sea).

(Other activities that could be chosen: ploughing and overgrazing, draining of wetlands, mining, and river channelisation.)

**Conclusion:** most activities that remove vegetation or cover the ground shorten the journey of water to the river and raise flood risk, whereas storage and abstraction change the amount and timing of the flow.

questions.enonce_markdown:
c) Briefly explain how climatic differences in Cameroon affect river regimes.

(9 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
A **river regime** is the pattern of seasonal variation in the discharge of a river through the year. It depends mainly on the **amount and seasonal distribution of rainfall**, and on temperature (which controls evapotranspiration), and so it follows the large climatic differences found in Cameroon.

**1. Southern Cameroon (equatorial climate: Guinean type).** Rain falls in **two wet seasons** (about March to June and September to November), separated by two shorter dry seasons, and no month is truly dry (total about 1,500 to 2,000 mm). Rivers such as the **Nyong, Ntem and Lobe** are perennial and carry a large volume of water, with **two high-water periods** following the two rainy seasons and a relatively small difference between high and low flow; the dense forest and the deep soils give a steady baseflow.

**2. The Centre and the transition zone (the Sanaga basin).** Where the rainfall is in one long season with a peak in September to October, the **Sanaga** has a **single main flood** in autumn (about September to November) and a clear low-water period (about February to March). Its size and the large catchment, and a lot of water stored in the soil and groundwater, make the flow smooth and the river perennial.

**3. The coast and the south-west (monsoon-type climate with very heavy rainfall).** Rainfall is among the highest in Africa (more than 3,000 mm, and more than 4,000 mm on the windward slopes of Mount Cameroon), with a long wet season from about June to October. Short, steep rivers such as the **Wouri, Mungo and Meme** have a **high discharge with a peak in the middle of the wet season (about July to September)** and a still substantial flow in the short dry season; floods are frequent.

**4. The Western Highlands.** Relief rainfall on the windward slopes gives a lot of water, but steep slopes and thin soils give a rapid response: the rivers are fast and rise quickly after storms, with a marked difference between wet and dry seasons.

**5. The North and Far North (tropical continental, Sudan and Sahel type).** There is **one short rainy season (about May or June to September or October)**, then a long dry season of 6 to 8 months, with high temperatures and high evapotranspiration. The **Benue, Logone and the mayos** (seasonal streams) have a **single sharp flood peak in August to September** and very low flow, or **no flow at all**, in the dry season (the mayos are intermittent: they flow only after rain, often as sudden floods). The flood of the Logone spreads over the flood plain (the *yaeres*), and the flow of the Benue is also controlled by the Lagdo dam, which stores the flood water and releases it in the dry season.

**Conclusion:** the more rain and the more evenly it is spread, the more regular and perennial the river (south: low coefficient of variation of flow); the shorter and more seasonal the rainfall, and the higher the evapotranspiration, the more contrasted the regime, up to intermittent flow (north). Human controls (dams such as Lagdo, Song Loulou and Edea on the Sanaga) modify the natural regime.
